0.title: Water, Bread and Wine
0.essay:
On the night before he died, Jesus did not leave his friends a book, a building or a set of rules for running an organisation. He took bread and a cup and said, “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). After he rose, he sent them out to make disciples, “baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Water, bread and wine: three of the plainest things in the world, given by the Lord of glory to carry the greatest news in the world.

Two gifts, often misunderstood

Few things Christians do are more familiar, and few are more argued over. Some churches baptise babies and some baptise only believers. Some sprinkle and some immerse. Some say the bread becomes Christ’s body, some say it reminds us of him, and others say something in between. Some take the Supper every week, some four times a year. Underneath the arguments, many ordinary church members are quietly unsure what is actually happening when the water is poured or the bread is broken.

This study is an attempt to slow down and look. It asks why Christ gave signs at all, what baptism and the Supper mean, how Christians have differed about them, and how they shape an ordinary week. Where faithful Christians disagree, each view is set out as its own friends would put it, and then this commentary’s view is given. This commentary holds the Reformed Baptist convictions of the 1689 Confession, and it honours as brothers and sisters the many godly believers who see these things differently.

The studies The Church (its chapters on baptism and the Lord’s Supper), Covenant Theology (on the baptism debate), Union with Christ and Worship & the Lord’s Day sit close by. This study goes further into the meaning of the two ordinances and the questions people actually ask about them.

The chapters

Visible Words: Why Christ Gave Signs; Buried and Raised: What Baptism Means; Who Should Be Baptised, and How; The Meal He Left Us; How Is Christ Present?; Coming to the Table; and Baptised People at One Table.

For reflection

What do you remember of your own baptism, or of the first time you took the Lord’s Supper? If a friend asked you what these two practices mean, what would you say, and where would you be unsure?

1.title: Visible Words: Why Christ Gave Signs
1.essay:
We are not only minds. God made us with eyes and hands and mouths, and he speaks to the whole of us. A husband tells his wife that he loves her. But on their wedding day he also put a ring on her finger, and on the hard days she looks at it. Christ has done something like that for his church.

God has always given signs

Throughout the Bible, God attaches visible signs to his promises. After the flood he said, “I have set my bow in the cloud, and it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and the earth” (Genesis 9:13). To Abraham he gave circumcision: “it shall be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (Genesis 17:11). On the night of the exodus the blood on the doorposts was a sign: “The blood shall be a sign for you, on the houses where you are. And when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13), and the Passover meal was kept every year afterwards to remember it.

The rainbow does not hold back the waters; God’s promise does. The sign does not make the promise true. It makes it visible, for people who forget easily and doubt often.

Signs and seals

Paul adds a second word. Abraham “received the sign of circumcision as a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith while he was still uncircumcised” (Romans 4:11). A sign points to something. A seal confirms it, like the wax seal a king pressed onto a letter to show that it really came from him. The seal did not create Abraham’s righteousness; it stamped God’s guarantee on it.

So the Westminster Confession calls baptism and the Supper “holy signs and seals of the covenant of grace”. They point to Christ, and they assure believers that what they point to is truly theirs.

The gospel you can see

Augustine, writing around the year 400, described a sacrament as a kind of visible word: the word of God joined to an ordinary thing, so that what we hear with our ears is shown to our eyes. Water without the word is just a bath, and bread without the word is just a snack. But water with Christ’s promise preaches, and bread with his words, “This is my body, which is for you” (1 Corinthians 11:24), proclaims his death.

Timothy Keller often pointed out that the gospel is not good advice but good news: not a list of things for us to do, but the announcement of something God has done. Baptism and the Supper are that news acted out. They are not mainly about our commitment or our feelings, but about God’s promise in Christ, set before us in water, bread and wine. “Oh, taste and see that the LORD is good!” (Psalm 34:8).

Sacrament or ordinance?

Christians use two words for these signs. Sacrament comes from the Latin sacramentum, a sacred pledge (it was used of a Roman soldier’s oath), and early Latin Bibles used it for the Greek word “mystery”. It stresses that God is at work in the sign. Ordinance means something ordained or commanded. It stresses that these are Christ’s appointments, which the church may not change, add to or drop.

The 1689 Baptist Confession calls baptism and the Supper ordinances, appointed by the Lord Jesus, the only lawgiver, to be continued in his church to the end of the world. Many Reformed Baptists happily use both words. What matters is not the label but the meaning: Christ commanded these signs, and Christ meets his people in them.

Seven or two?

The Roman Catholic Church counts seven sacraments: baptism, confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, holy orders and marriage, a list confirmed at the Council of Trent. The Orthodox churches also speak of seven holy mysteries, though they hold the number more loosely. They want God’s grace to mark the whole of life, from birth to death, and grace does reach every part of life.

The Reformers asked a narrower question: which signs did Christ himself institute, with a visible element and a gospel promise, for the whole church to keep until he comes? Only two meet that test. Marriage is a precious gift of creation, given to believers and unbelievers alike; Paul calls it a “mystery” that “refers to Christ and the church” (Ephesians 5:32), but he does not make it a sacrament of the church. Jesus washed his disciples’ feet as “an example” of humble love (John 13:15), not a new sign. This commentary holds that Christ gave two ordinances, baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

The God who stoops

Why would the God who needs nothing bother with water and bread? John Calvin answered that God, in his kindness, comes down to our level, as a parent stoops to a small child. We are slow to believe, and creatures of sight and touch. So he does not only tell us that we are washed; he washes us. He does not only tell us that Christ is food for our souls; he puts bread in our hands.

And this is only an echo of the greatest thing God ever did to be seen. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory” (John 1:14). The eternal Son did not stay a voice from heaven. He took a body that could be touched, broken and raised. Baptism and the Supper are small, plain signs of that great humility.

A man in his fifties, who had always found reading hard, sat through sermons feeling that the gospel was something for cleverer people. The day he watched a friend go down into the water and come up again, he turned to his wife and said, “I understood that.” He had heard the words for years. Now he could see them.

For reflection

Why do you think God attaches visible signs to his promises? What is the difference between a sign and a seal? Which word, “sacrament” or “ordinance”, has your church tended to use, and what does each one help you see? How might it change your next communion Sunday to think of it as the gospel you can see and taste?

2.title: Buried and Raised: What Baptism Means
2.essay:
Some Christians in Rome were asking a dangerous question. If grace is greater than all our sin, why not keep on sinning? Paul’s answer was to remind them of their baptism: “Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” (Romans 6:3). He expected their baptism to tell them who they were.

Into his death and out again

“We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, in order that, just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). Baptism is a picture of union with Christ. When a believer goes down under the water, it is like a burial. When he comes up, it is like a resurrection. The old life, the person we were outside Christ, has died with him. A new life, his risen life, has begun.

This is more than a vivid image. What happened to Christ counts as having happened to those who belong to him: his death is their death, his rising their rising. So Paul concludes, “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:11). Baptism does not create that union; faith receives it. But baptism shows it, seals it and calls us to live it.

The baptism Jesus dreaded

To see the depth of this sign, look at Jesus’ own baptism. He came to John the Baptist at the Jordan, and John tried to stop him: “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” (Matthew 3:14). John’s baptism was for repentance, and Jesus had nothing to repent of. But he stepped into the water among sinners, taking his place with them. And as he came up, the Spirit descended and the Father spoke: “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17). Father, Son and Spirit together: the whole Trinity at the riverbank.

Later Jesus spoke of another baptism: “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!” (Luke 12:50). He was speaking of the cross. In the Old Testament, deep waters are often a picture of overwhelming judgment and sorrow. The psalmist cries, “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Psalm 42:7), and Jonah in the sea uses almost the same words. On the cross the full flood of God’s judgment against sin went over the head of his Son.

This is why Scripture links baptism with the flood and the Red Sea. In Noah’s day eight people “were brought safely through water” (1 Peter 3:20), and Israel “passed through the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1). The waters that destroyed God’s enemies carried his people through. When a believer goes under the water of baptism, he is not drowned, because Christ has already gone under the real waters for him. Our baptism is gentle because his was not.

Washed

Water washes, and baptism speaks of cleansing from sin. God had promised through Ezekiel, “I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean from all your uncleannesses” (Ezekiel 36:25). Paul reminds the Corinthians of what some of them had been, and then says, “But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (1 Corinthians 6:11). Hebrews speaks of believers having “our hearts sprinkled clean from an evil conscience and our bodies washed with pure water” (Hebrews 10:22).

The water itself removes nothing but dirt. What cleanses is what it points to: “the blood of Jesus his Son cleanses us from all sin” (1 John 1:7). But a believer who feels stained can remember the day he was washed in Christ’s name, and know that what it signified is complete.

Into the name

Jesus told his disciples to baptise “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Notice: one name, not three names. To be baptised into that name is to be marked as belonging to the one God who is Father, Son and Spirit. It is a little like a bride taking her husband’s name. She is now known as his. Paul uses another picture: “For as many of you as were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Galatians 3:27). Baptism is like being clothed in Christ, so that when God looks at us he sees his Son.

Into one body

Baptism is never a private ceremony. “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). The Spirit’s work joins every believer to Christ’s body, and water baptism is the visible doorway into the local church that is the visible form of that body. That is why baptism usually happens in front of the congregation, and why the baptised are welcomed into membership and to the Lord’s table. You are not baptised into a feeling; you are baptised into a family.

A funeral and a birthday

A man in his thirties came to faith after years of drugs and broken relationships. On the morning of his baptism he told the pastor that he felt like a fraud. The pastor reminded him that baptism was about Christ’s death and resurrection, not his own past. As he went under the water he thought, “That man is buried.” As he came up, the church was singing. He said afterwards that it had felt like a funeral and a birthday at the same time. Years later, on bad days, he still goes back to that morning in his mind.

For reflection

How does Romans 6:3–4 change the way you think about sin and temptation? What does it mean to you that Jesus went under the waters of judgment so that baptism could be a sign of mercy? Why does baptism belong in the gathered church rather than in private? If you are baptised, which part of its meaning do you most need to remember this week?

3.title: Who Should Be Baptised, and How
3.essay:
Here is one of the oldest family disagreements among Christians who love the Bible. Two believers can agree on almost everything about the gospel, read the same Scriptures with the same seriousness, and still disagree about whether a baby should be baptised. That should make us humble, careful and kind.

What is shared

Reformed Christians on both sides agree on what baptism means, that it does not save by itself, and that the children of believers are greatly privileged. The study Covenant Theology sets out the covenant arguments in detail; here we summarise them and ask what they mean in church life.

The case for infant baptism

Most of the historic Reformed churches, together with Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches, baptise the infants of believers. Reformed paedobaptists (from the Greek for “child”) argue first from the unity of God’s covenant. God promised Abraham “to be God to you and to your offspring after you” (Genesis 17:7), and the sign was given to infants. The covenant of grace is one, and nowhere does the New Testament put children outside it.

Second, baptism takes the place of circumcision. Paul says believers were “circumcised with a circumcision made without hands … having been buried with him in baptism” (Colossians 2:11–12). Third, the apostles baptised households: Lydia “was baptized, and her household as well” (Acts 16:15), and the Philippian jailer “was baptized at once, he and all his family” (Acts 16:33). Fourth, Peter said, “the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:39), and Paul calls the children of a believing parent “holy” (1 Corinthians 7:14).

At its best this view expresses a deep sense of grace. The sign declares God’s promise before our response, as circumcision was given to Isaac before he could believe: God’s mercy comes first. Calvin and many of the church’s finest pastors held it with a clear conscience and a warm heart.

The case for believers’ baptism

Credobaptists (from the Latin for “I believe”) see a different pattern: every baptism the New Testament describes follows hearing and believing. “Those who received his word were baptized” (Acts 2:41). In Samaria, “when they believed Philip as he preached good news … they were baptized, both men and women” (Acts 8:12).

The new covenant is new in exactly this point. God promised a covenant not like the old, in which “they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34). Its members are joined by new birth, not natural birth. Colossians 2 says believers were raised with Christ “through faith” (Colossians 2:12): the counterpart of circumcision is the circumcision of the heart, and baptism is its sign. Peter’s promise is to “everyone whom the Lord our God calls to himself” (Acts 2:39). And in Philippi the word was spoken “to all who were in his house” (Acts 16:32), and the jailer rejoiced “along with his entire household that he had believed in God” (Acts 16:34).

This commentary’s view: with the 1689 Confession, baptism is for those who credibly profess repentance towards God and faith in the Lord Jesus. The sign of union with Christ by faith belongs to those who have come to Christ by faith. Paedobaptist believers are honoured brothers and sisters; we will sit together at the marriage supper of the Lamb, and we can learn from each other now.

How much water?

The Greek word baptizō ordinarily means to dip or immerse. When Philip baptised the Ethiopian official, “they both went down into the water” and came “up out of the water” (Acts 8:38–39). Going under and coming up pictures burial and resurrection most clearly. So this commentary holds that immersion is the norm. Yet the early Christian manual called the Didache already allowed pouring when water was scarce, and the meaning of baptism does not depend on the amount of water.

Does baptism make us born again?

Roman Catholic, Orthodox and Lutheran Christians, and some Anglicans, believe that baptism conveys new birth. They point to strong texts: “unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5); “Repent and be baptized … for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts 2:38); the “washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5); “Baptism … now saves you” (1 Peter 3:21). They want to honour Christ’s promise as objective.

This commentary agrees that God really acts in baptism: he signs and seals his promise. But Scripture does not tie new birth to the water. Cornelius and his household received the Holy Spirit before they were baptised, which is exactly why Peter asked, “Can anyone withhold water for baptizing these people, who have received the Holy Spirit just as we have?” (Acts 10:47). The thief on the cross was promised paradise without baptism. Simon the sorcerer was baptised, yet Peter told him, “your heart is not right before God” (Acts 8:21). Paul could hardly have said, “Christ did not send me to baptize but to preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 1:17), if baptism were the moment of new birth. And Peter himself explains that baptism saves “not as a removal of dirt from the body but as an appeal to God for a good conscience” (1 Peter 3:21). Sign and reality are so closely tied that Scripture speaks of them together, but the reality comes through faith.

If you were baptised as a baby

Many believers were baptised as infants by parents who loved Christ and prayed for them. If you have come to believers’ baptism, being baptised now is not an insult to them; their prayers have been answered. In this commentary’s view it is your first true baptism, not a second one, because baptism is the sign of the faith you now have. When some disciples in Ephesus learned that the baptism they had received was not yet baptism into Jesus, “they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 19:5). Talk it through with your elders, take your time, and act from conviction, not pressure.

A woman in her forties had been baptised as a baby by parents who served their church faithfully for decades. When she came to believers’ baptism, she feared hurting her mother. She thanked her for every prayer and explained that she wanted to obey Christ as she understood Scripture. Her mother did not agree, but she came. Afterwards she said, “I prayed for this day, even if it does not look like the day I imagined.”

For reflection

What do Christians on both sides of the baptism debate agree on, and why does that matter? Which argument on the other side do you find strongest, and why? How can you speak about baptism with a Christian who differs, in a way that honours both the truth and them?

4.title: The Meal He Left Us
4.essay:
Hours before his arrest, with the cross in full view, Jesus said to his friends, “I have earnestly desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer” (Luke 22:15). He was not dreading this meal. He had longed for it. And at that table he gave his church a meal of its own, to keep until he comes again.

The night it began

The Lord’s Supper was born inside the Passover. Every year Israel ate the lamb, the unleavened bread and the bitter herbs to remember the night God struck Egypt and passed over the houses marked with blood. God had told them, “This day shall be for you a memorial day” (Exodus 12:14). He even built a question into the meal: “when your children say to you, ‘What do you mean by this service?’ you shall say, ‘It is the sacrifice of the LORD’s Passover’” (Exodus 12:26–27). Families reclined together at the table (see Meals and Reclining at Table), and each generation was taught to see itself among those whom God had rescued.

Into that ancient meal Jesus spoke astonishing words. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said, “This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22:19). Then the cup: “This cup that is poured out for you is the new covenant in my blood” (Luke 22:20). The true Passover lamb was at the table. Paul puts it plainly: “For Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The exodus from Egypt was a shadow. The real rescue, from sin and death and judgment, was about to happen on a hill outside Jerusalem.

A covenant meal

When God made his covenant with Israel at Sinai, Moses sprinkled the people with blood, and then the elders went up the mountain: “they beheld God, and ate and drank” (Exodus 24:11). A covenant was sealed with blood and celebrated with a meal. At the Last Supper Jesus said, “this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). The Supper is the meal of the new covenant, promised through Jeremiah, in which God forgives sin and remembers it no more. Each time we eat it, that promise is set before us again.

Many names, one meal

The Bible and the church have several names for this meal, and each catches something. Paul calls it “the Lord’s supper” (1 Corinthians 11:20): it is his meal, and he is the host. Luke calls it “the breaking of bread” (Acts 2:42), a reminder that it is a real, shared meal. “Communion” comes from Paul’s word for “participation” (1 Corinthians 10:16). And the old name Eucharist comes from the Greek word for giving thanks, because Jesus took the bread “when he had given thanks” (Luke 22:19). It is a meal of gratitude.

Remembering

“Do this in remembrance of me.” In the Bible, remembering is much more than calling a fact to mind. When God “remembers” his covenant, he acts on it. When Israel remembered the exodus, they were not studying history; they were taking their place in it. So when the church remembers Christ, it is not like looking at an old photograph. It is setting ourselves again at the foot of the cross, receiving afresh the love that was poured out there, and living from it.

This is a mercy, because the worries of a week push Christ’s death to the edge of our minds, and the Supper pulls it back to the centre.

Proclaiming

“For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). The Supper is a sermon you can taste. Even if no word were spoken, the broken bread and poured cup would announce that the Son of God gave his body and shed his blood for sinners. A church at the table preaches the gospel to itself, to its children and to any visitor who wonders what is going on.

Sharing

“The bread that we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ? Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:16–17). The Supper is not only something we do about Christ; it is a sharing in Christ, and with one another. Chapter 5 asks how Christ is present, and the last chapter how the meal binds his people together.

Looking ahead

Jesus also said, “I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom” (Matthew 26:29). The Supper is a meal for travellers who are not home yet. Isaiah saw the end of the story as a banquet: “On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine” (Isaiah 25:6), and on that mountain God “will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:8). John heard the angel say, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9). Every small piece of bread and sip from the cup is a taste of that feast, a promise on the tongue that the best is still to come.

A Passover fulfilled

A man who grew up in a Jewish family kept the Passover every spring as a boy. As the youngest, he used to ask the traditional questions about why this night was different. Years later, after he came to trust Jesus as the Messiah, he took the Lord’s Supper for the first time. When the minister read, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed”, he wept quietly. He said afterwards, “I had been asking the question all my life. That night I heard the answer.”

For reflection

What does the Passover background add to your understanding of the Lord’s Supper? How is biblical remembering different from simply recalling a fact? In what sense is the Supper a sermon? How might looking ahead to the marriage supper of the Lamb change the way you come to the table?

5.title: How Is Christ Present?
5.essay:
“Take, eat; this is my body” (Matthew 26:26). Few sentences in history have been argued over more. The question is not hair-splitting: it touches Christ’s true humanity, the finished nature of his sacrifice, and what faith receives at his table.

What all agree on

Christians who differ here agree that Christ gave the Supper, that it proclaims his death until he returns, and that in some real way he meets his people in it. The disagreement is about how. Four main answers have been given, and each deserves to be heard as its own friends would put it.

Rome: transubstantiation

The Roman Catholic Church teaches that when the priest speaks Christ’s words over the bread and wine, their substance, what they really are, is changed into the body and blood of Christ, while their appearance stays the same. The term was used by the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, and the Council of Trent defined the doctrine. Catholic teaching also holds that the Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Calvary in an unbloody way, not a new sacrifice. Catholics take Jesus’ words at their plainest, and John 6 with great seriousness: “unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you” (John 6:53). The Orthodox also believe the bread and wine truly become Christ’s body and blood, but prefer to call it a mystery rather than define it.

Luther: in, with and under

Martin Luther rejected transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the Mass, but he would not let go of the word “is”. At Marburg in 1529 he met the Swiss Reformer Ulrich Zwingli; they agreed on almost every point of doctrine, but not this one, and Luther is said to have chalked “This is my body” in Latin on the table. Lutherans teach that Christ’s true body and blood are present “in, with and under” the bread and wine, which remain bread and wine (they dislike the label “consubstantiation”). Their concern is precious: Christ’s gift at the table is objective, there because he promised it, not because we feel the right things.

Zwingli: a memorial

Zwingli argued that “is” here means “signifies”, as in many other places in Scripture. Christ’s body, he said, is in heaven, and “the flesh is no help at all” (John 6:63). The Supper is a memorial of Christ’s death, a thanksgiving, and the congregation’s public pledge of loyalty to Christ and to one another. Many evangelicals hold a view close to his. It was richer than the label “mere memorial” suggests, and its great strength is that it guards Christ’s once-for-all sacrifice from any hint of repetition.

Calvin: present by the Spirit

John Calvin agreed with Zwingli that Christ’s body is in heaven, and with Luther that the Supper is far more than a reminder. Christ’s human body remains in heaven, “whom heaven must receive until the time for restoring all the things” (Acts 3:21). But the Holy Spirit unites us to the whole Christ, so that at his table believers truly feed on him by faith. Calvin made much of the ancient call in the church’s liturgy, “Lift up your hearts”: Christ does not come down into the bread; by the Spirit our hearts are lifted up to him. The signs are not empty: with them God gives what they signify to all who receive them in faith.

The 1689 Baptist Confession, following the Westminster Confession almost word for word, teaches that believers who receive the bread and wine in faith inwardly feed on Christ crucified and all the benefits of his death, “really and indeed, yet not carnally and corporally, but spiritually”.

This commentary’s view

This commentary’s view: the Reformed view, that Christ is truly present by his Spirit and believers truly feed on him by faith, while the bread and wine remain what they are, fits the whole of Scripture best.

First, the Bible often speaks of a sign as if it were the thing it signifies. God called circumcision “my covenant” (Genesis 17:10), though it was the sign of the covenant. Jesus said, “I am the door” (John 10:9) and “I am the true vine” (John 15:1), and no one thinks he became wood or a plant. “This is my body” is that kind of speech.

Second, Christ’s humanity is real and remains real. He was “carried up into heaven” (Luke 24:51) in the body, and he will return “in the same way” (Acts 1:11). A body in ten thousand places at once would hardly be human like ours. And his sacrifice is finished: “when Christ had offered for all time a single sacrifice for sins, he sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:12). Nothing needs to be offered again.

Third, the Supper is more than a memory. Paul calls it “a participation in the body of Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:16). In John 6, eating Christ is explained as coming to him and believing: “whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). Faith eats. By the Spirit, the believing heart is nourished by the living Christ as surely as the body is by bread.

So the Reformed view keeps what each of the others rightly guards: Christ’s real gift, his real body and his finished work. Catholic and Lutheran Christians often shame others by their reverence at the table, and memorialists rightly let nothing rival the cross. We can learn from them all.

Better that he went

Jesus told his disciples, “it is to your advantage that I go away, for if I do not go away, the Helper will not come to you” (John 16:7). A Man with a real human body sits at the right hand of the Father, and yet by his Spirit he is with every one of his people, in every place, at once. The table does not bring him down from heaven. It lifts us up to him.

A woman raised a devout Catholic joined an evangelical church and was troubled by how casual the Supper seemed. “Do you think he is actually here?” she asked an elder. He explained the Reformed view. She said, “So it is not less than I was taught. It is different, and it is about him.”

For reflection

Which concern of each view (Catholic, Lutheran, memorial, Reformed) do you find most worth guarding? How does Genesis 17:10 help us read “This is my body”? Why does it matter that Christ’s body is a true human body in heaven? What would it look like for you to “lift up your heart” at the next Lord’s Supper?

6.title: Coming to the Table
6.essay:
The plate comes along the row, and something in you hesitates. Am I good enough this week? What if I take it wrongly? The Lord’s Supper is meant to be a feast, but for some believers it has become a monthly test they are afraid of failing.

Who may come

The table is the Lord’s, so he sets the guest list: baptised believers who trust Christ, who are not under the discipline of a church, and who examine themselves as Paul commands. In this commentary’s view they are welcome whatever congregation they belong to, because it is Christ’s table, not ours. Those who have not yet trusted Christ should not eat, but they are very welcome to be present, to watch and to ask what it means.

What about children? In this commentary’s view a child who credibly professes faith should be baptised and then welcomed to the table. Some Christians give the Supper to young children of believers (paedocommunion), and the Orthodox give it to baptised infants, wanting to show that children belong to God’s family. But Paul asks those who eat to examine themselves and discern the body, which requires a faith of one’s own. And a believer with dementia, who has professed faith for many years and can no longer explain it, should not be turned away. Christ holds them when their memory cannot.

“In an unworthy manner”

The words that frighten people most are these: “Whoever, therefore, eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord in an unworthy manner will be guilty concerning the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:27). Read them in their setting. In Corinth the wealthy were feasting and getting drunk while the poor went hungry. Paul is angry: “do you despise the church of God and humiliate those who have nothing?” (1 Corinthians 11:22). That was the unworthy manner: treating Christ’s death and Christ’s people with contempt.

Notice that Paul says “in an unworthy manner”, not “if you are unworthy”. No one is worthy. The Supper is not a prize for the spiritually successful but medicine for the sick. Jesus said, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners” (Mark 2:17). A story is often told of John Duncan, a nineteenth-century Scottish minister, who saw a woman weeping and refusing the cup because she felt too sinful. He leaned over and told her, in effect, to take it, because it was for sinners. Her tears showed she was the very person the table was for.

Examine, then eat

“Let a person examine himself, then, and so eat of the bread and drink of the cup” (1 Corinthians 11:28). The goal of self-examination is not staying away but eating. We look honestly at our sin in order to bring it to Christ, not to find ourselves fit. Paul adds that we must discern “the body” (1 Corinthians 11:29). That probably means both recognising the Lord’s body given for us and recognising his body the church gathered around us, whom the Corinthians were despising.

Even God’s discipline here is kind: “when we are judged by the Lord, we are disciplined so that we may not be condemned along with the world” (1 Corinthians 11:32). Someone clinging to sin he refuses to give up, or to hatred he will not lay down, should not eat lightly. But the one who comes troubled, repentant and hungry is not eating judgment. He is eating grace.

Fencing the table

In older Scottish churches the minister “fenced the table”: he spelled out who should not come, then invited those who should. Done badly, this frightened tender consciences and emboldened the proud. Done well, it is pastoral love: a brief explanation, a warning to those not trusting Christ or living in deliberate sin, and a warm welcome to every weak, struggling believer.

How often?

The first Christians devoted themselves to “the breaking of bread” (Acts 2:42), and in Troas they gathered “On the first day of the week … to break bread” (Acts 20:7). Calvin wanted the Supper every Lord’s Day, but the Geneva city council allowed it only four times a year. Scripture commands no frequency, and churches are free here. This commentary’s view is that weekly communion is a great blessing, and that what matters most is coming in faith.

Getting ready

On the evening before, read one of the Gospel accounts of the cross. Confess particular sins to God, and thank him for particular mercies. If you know someone has something against you, try to put it right, as Jesus said: “First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift” (Matthew 5:24). Then come hungry. God’s invitation has always been for the empty-handed: “Come, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money, come, buy and eat!” (Isaiah 55:1).

For the anxious and the scrupulous

Some believers are tormented by a constant fear that they have sinned unknowingly or not confessed perfectly, and stay away from the table for months or years. If that is you, you are not alone. Talk to your pastor, and ask for a biblical counsellor, through your church or an organisation such as ACBC or CCEF in the United States or Biblical Counselling UK. A good counsellor will open God’s sufficient Word with you, and will also ask you to see your doctor, because repetitive, intrusive fears can have a physical side too. Medical treatment is no failure of faith. And in the meantime, the Supper is for you.

A man in his forties had not taken communion for three years. Every time he examined himself, he found more sin and felt he had to confess again. His elder met with him over many weeks, alongside a counsellor, and read 1 Corinthians 11:28 with him slowly: “examine himself, then, and so eat”. One Sunday he took the bread with shaking hands. He said afterwards, “I came as the sick man. That was the point.”

For reflection

Have you ever hesitated to come to the table? Why? What does “in an unworthy manner” mean in its setting, and what does it not mean? How can self-examination lead you towards the table rather than away from it? What could you do this week to prepare for the next Lord’s Supper?

7.title: Baptised People at One Table
7.essay:
Baptism happens once. The Supper comes round again and again. But neither is meant to stay in the church building. They tell us who we are on Monday morning, in the car, at the office, alone late at night. Christ gave them to shape a whole life.

I am baptised

Martin Luther knew dark seasons of temptation and accusation. He taught that when sin and the devil press on our conscience, the Christian should answer, in effect: But I am baptised. He did not mean the water was magic, but that God had put his name and promise on him, and that this outward word was stronger than the inward voice of accusation.

This commentary does not share Luther’s view that baptism gives new birth, but it shares his comfort. A believer’s baptism is God’s visible pledge that he belongs to Christ: died with him, raised with him, washed, clothed in him. That is why Paul, facing Christians tempted to treat sin lightly, did not first give them a technique. He told them who they were: “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:11). When temptation or accusation says, “This is who you really are”, the baptised believer can answer, “No. I have been washed. I bear another name now.”

A woman who had been a Christian for twenty years still lay awake some nights replaying a cruel thing she had done as a teenager. A voice inside said that God could never really have accepted someone like her. One night she remembered standing in the water as her pastor baptised her in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. God had put his own name on her, knowing everything about her. “I have been washed,” she whispered, and slept. If shame like hers keeps returning and darkens your days, do not carry it alone: talk to your pastor, and see the study Shame.

One baptism, one bread

Both ordinances are also deeply shared. “There is one body and one Spirit … one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all” (Ephesians 4:4–6). Everyone baptised into Christ has been baptised into the same name, and everyone at the table eats from the same loaf: “we who are many are one body, for we all partake of the one bread” (1 Corinthians 10:17).

This is why the Corinthians’ divided tables appalled Paul. Rich and poor were eating separately. He told them bluntly, “When you come together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat” (1 Corinthians 11:20). A Supper that keeps the walls of class, race or friendship groups standing is not really the Lord’s Supper at all. The table levels us. The company director and the man who sleeps in the night shelter hold out the same empty hands and receive the same bread. “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28).

So the ordinances push us into one another’s lives. It is hard to share the bread on Sunday and refuse to speak to someone on Monday. The Supper invites reconciliation, and the table in church spills over into the tables in our homes, where the lonely, the new and the overlooked can be welcomed.

Until he comes

Baptism looks back to a day; the Supper looks forward to one. We “proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26). Christians are pilgrims with a meal for the road, and the meal reminds them where the road ends: at a wedding (see Weddings and Betrothal), the “marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

The host and the meal

Step back now and see who stands at the centre of both signs. In baptism we see the Christ who went down into the deep waters of judgment, so that our waters could be waters of mercy. At the table we see the Christ who prayed in the garden, “Remove this cup from me. Yet not what I will, but what you will” (Mark 14:36). He drank the cup of God’s wrath to the bottom so that we could drink the cup of blessing.

And he is not only the one who gives the meal. He is the meal. “I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst” (John 6:35). Every other bread is eaten and gone, and we are hungry again. He feeds us with himself, and he is never used up.

He is also the host. At the Last Supper, while the disciples argued about who was greatest, he said, “I am among you as the one who serves” (Luke 22:27). And here is the most astonishing promise of all. Jesus said that when the master returns and finds his servants waiting, “he will dress himself for service and have them recline at table, and he will come and serve them” (Luke 12:37). At the last feast, the King of glory will not only sit at the head of the table. He will get up and serve his guests.

Think of it. The water closing over a believer, the bread placed in a trembling hand, the cup passed along a row of ordinary people on an ordinary Sunday: all of it is a pledge from the Son of God that he has washed us, that he feeds us, and that one day he will seat us at his own table and wait on us himself, while God “will wipe away tears from all faces” (Isaiah 25:8). We are baptised people, and we eat together, because we belong to him.

For reflection

When temptation or accusation comes, how could remembering your baptism help you to answer it? What walls in your church might the Lord’s Supper be challenging? Who could you welcome to your own table in the coming weeks? How does it move you that Christ is both the host and the meal, and that he will one day serve his people himself?
